meta.name: Policy catalog
meta.note: Original policy text written for this site. Tiers follow CIS Implementation Groups and are additive: an IG2 policy includes every IG1 statement, and IG3 includes both. Placeholders in {{braces}} are substituted from the organization profile.

tiers.name: IG1
tiers.blurb: Essential cyber hygiene. The floor every organization should reach, achievable without a dedicated security team.

tiers.name: IG2
tiers.blurb: Adds the practices an organization needs once it has staff dedicated to security and regulated or sensitive data.

tiers.name: IG3
tiers.blurb: Adds the practices expected where a breach would be material: formal assurance, independent testing, and measured effectiveness.

policies.title: Information Security Policy
policies.summary: The parent policy. States that {{org}} runs a security program, who owns it, and what everyone is accountable for.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes {{org}}'s commitment to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the information and systems it depends on. It sets the authority under which every other security policy is issued.
policies.scope: All workers, contractors, and third parties acting on behalf of {{org}}, and all information and systems {{org}} owns or operates, regardless of location or ownership of the device.

roles.responsibility: Approves this policy, accepts residual risk on behalf of {{org}}, and provides the funding and authority the program needs to function.
Owns the security program, maintains this and subordinate policies, and reports posture and material risks to leadership.
Classify the information they are accountable for and ensure the controls required by this policy are implemented in their systems.
Follow these policies, complete required training, and report suspected security issues promptly.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a documented information security program, approved by executive leadership and reviewed at least {{review}}.
A named individual, {{owner}}, is formally accountable for the security program. The role is documented and the appointment is current.
This policy and its subordinate policies are published where all workers can reach them, and workers are told when a material change is made.
Every worker acknowledges these policies on hire and again {{review}}.
{{org}} maintains an inventory of the systems and information it depends on, sufficient to know what the program is protecting.
Security risks that leadership chooses not to remediate are recorded, with the reason, the accepting executive, and a review date.
Suspected security issues can be reported by any worker through a documented channel, without fear of reprisal.
Violations of this policy are handled through {{org}}'s normal disciplinary process.
ig2: {{org}} maintains a risk register covering its material information security risks, each with an owner, a treatment decision, and a review date.
Risk assessments are performed at least {{review}} and on significant change to systems, suppliers, or the regulatory environment.
Security objectives are documented and progress against them is reported to leadership at least quarterly.
Subordinate policies name a single accountable owner and carry a review date.
Roles with security responsibilities are defined in writing, including segregation between those who request access and those who grant it.
ig3: The security program is assessed against a named external framework at least {{review}}, and findings are tracked to closure.
An independent party reviews the program's effectiveness at least {{review}}, and the results go to leadership without filtering.
Leadership reviews measured control effectiveness, not only control existence, when accepting risk.
Exceptions to policy are time-bound, individually approved, and expire automatically unless renewed.

policies.exceptions: Any exception to this policy must be requested in writing, justified by business need, approved by {{owner}}, recorded with a compensating control and an expiry date, and reviewed before renewal.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and on any material change to {{org}}'s business, systems, or regulatory obligations.
evidence: The approved policy document, with approval date and approver
The current policy acknowledgement record
The risk register and the most recent risk assessment
Minutes or a report showing leadership review of security posture

policies.title: Access Control Policy
policies.summary: Who may reach which systems and data, how that access is granted, reviewed, and removed.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how access to {{org}}'s systems and information is requested, approved, provisioned, reviewed, and revoked, so that people hold only the access their role requires.
policies.scope: All accounts on all systems {{org}} owns or subscribes to, including cloud services, and all workers, contractors, and service accounts that hold them.

roles.responsibility: Define the access roles available on their system and approve or deny access requests.
Maintains this policy, runs access reviews, and investigates access that cannot be justified.
Notifies system owners of joiners, movers, and leavers in time for access to be granted or removed.
Use only the access granted to them, and never share credentials.

ig1: Access is granted on the principle of least privilege: a worker receives only the access their role requires, and no more.
Every access grant is approved by the owner of the system or data before it is provisioned.
Access is granted to named individual accounts. Shared accounts are used only where a system cannot support individual accounts, and each is documented with a named owner.
Access is revoked on the same business day a worker leaves {{org}}, and adjusted when they change role.
{{org}} maintains a current list of accounts with administrative access to each system.
Default and vendor-supplied accounts are disabled, removed, or have their credentials changed before a system is used.
Service accounts are documented with a named human owner and the purpose they serve.
ig2: Access rights are reviewed at least {{review}} by the relevant system owner, and access that cannot be justified is removed.
Access is granted through defined roles rather than assembled per person, so that a role change is a single action.
Dormant accounts are disabled after a defined period of inactivity.
Elevated access is granted separately from day-to-day access, so administrators do not browse the web or read mail from a privileged account.
Access to systems holding regulated or confidential data requires documented approval from the data owner in addition to the system owner.
ig3: Elevated access is granted just in time and expires automatically, rather than standing permanently.
Access reviews are evidenced with the reviewer, date, and the disposition of each account, and are retained for audit.
Access grants and revocations are logged and reconciled against the joiner, mover, and leaver record at least quarterly.
Segregation of duties conflicts are defined in writing and enforced or explicitly compensated.

policies.exceptions: Access that departs from this policy requires written approval from {{owner}} and the relevant data owner, a documented compensating control, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a system that materially changes how access is managed.
evidence: Access request and approval records
The most recent access review, with reviewer and disposition per account
A current list of privileged accounts
Leaver records showing revocation timing

policies.title: Incident Response Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} detects, declares, contains, and learns from security incidents, and who decides what.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} prepares for and responds to security incidents, so that response is decided in advance rather than improvised under pressure.
policies.scope: Any event that compromises, or credibly threatens to compromise, the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of {{org}}'s information or systems, including events at a supplier that affect {{org}}.

roles.responsibility: Runs the response, makes containment decisions, and is the single point of coordination for the duration of an incident.
Maintains this policy and the response plan, and appoints the incident commander for each incident.
Decides on external notification, regulatory reporting, and any payment or legal action.
Report suspected incidents immediately and preserve evidence rather than attempting to remediate alone.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a written incident response plan that names who to contact, in what order, at any hour.
Every worker knows how to report a suspected incident, and reporting is possible without going through the worker's own manager.
Incidents are recorded with what happened, when it was detected, what was done, and who decided.
A named individual has authority to declare an incident and to take systems offline to contain it.
{{org}} knows which regulators, customers, or insurers it may be obliged to notify, and within what deadline, before an incident occurs.
Contact details for law enforcement, legal counsel, and any cyber insurer are recorded and reachable outside normal business hours.
After a significant incident, {{org}} performs a review and records what will change as a result.
ig2: The incident response plan is tested at least {{review}} through a tabletop or live exercise, and the plan is updated with what the exercise found.
Incidents are classified by severity using documented criteria, and severity drives escalation and notification timing.
{{org}} maintains the ability to preserve logs and forensic evidence before remediating, where doing so does not prolong material harm.
Response roles have named alternates, so a single person's absence does not stall the response.
Third-party incidents affecting {{org}} are handled under this policy, and supplier contracts require prompt notification.
ig3: {{org}} measures and reports mean time to detect and mean time to contain, and treats adverse trends as findings.
Post-incident actions are tracked to closure with named owners and dates, and closure is verified rather than asserted.
Exercises include at least one scenario per year that assumes a control failed rather than held.
An external party is retained in advance for forensic support, so engagement does not begin during an incident.

policies.exceptions: Deviation from the response plan during an active incident is permitted where the incident commander judges it necessary, and must be recorded in the incident log and reviewed afterwards.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, after any significant incident, and after any exercise that identifies a gap.
evidence: The current incident response plan, with version and approval date
Incident records for the review period
Exercise records, including what changed as a result
Post-incident review findings and their closure status

policies.title: Data Classification and Protection Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} classifies information and what handling each class requires, through its whole life.
policies.purpose: This policy defines how {{org}} classifies information by sensitivity and what protection each class requires at rest, in transit, in use, and at disposal.
policies.scope: All information {{org}} creates, receives, stores, or transmits, in any form, including information held on {{org}}'s behalf by a supplier.

roles.responsibility: Assign a classification to the information they are accountable for and approve who may access it.
Maintains the classification scheme and the handling requirements for each class.
Handle information according to its classification and do not move it to unapproved services or devices.

ig1: {{org}} uses a documented classification scheme with a small number of clearly distinguished levels.
Information holding personal, financial, or otherwise regulated data is identified and classified at the highest level {{org}} operates.
Handling requirements are documented for each classification level, covering storage, sharing, transmission, and disposal.
Confidential information is encrypted in transit over any network {{org}} does not control.
Portable devices and removable media that hold confidential information are encrypted at rest.
Information is disposed of so that it cannot be reconstructed, and disposal of confidential information is recorded.
{{org}} knows, for each class of regulated information it holds, which systems hold it.
ig2: Confidential information is encrypted at rest wherever the storage platform supports it.
Retention periods are defined per classification and enforced, so information is not kept indefinitely by default.
Approved locations are defined for each classification, and workers are told which services are not approved.
Data flows carrying regulated information to third parties are documented, including the legal basis or contract that permits the transfer.
Production data is not used in development or test environments unless it has been masked or de-identified.
ig3: Automated controls detect and alert on confidential information leaving approved locations.
Encryption keys are managed under a documented lifecycle, with defined rotation and separation from the data they protect.
The classification of high-value information is validated at least {{review}} rather than assumed to be still correct.
Disposal of confidential information is evidenced by certificate or verifiable log.

policies.exceptions: Handling information outside the requirements for its classification requires written approval from the data owner and {{owner}}, a compensating control, and an expiry date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} begins processing a new category of regulated information.
evidence: The classification scheme and its handling matrix
An inventory of systems holding regulated information
Encryption configuration for systems holding confidential data
Retention and disposal records

policies.title: Third-Party and Supplier Security Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} evaluates suppliers before trusting them, and what it requires of them afterwards.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} assesses and manages the security risk introduced by suppliers, service providers, and any third party that accesses its information or systems.
policies.scope: All third parties that store, process, or transmit {{org}}'s information, or that hold access to its systems, including subprocessors engaged by those parties.

roles.responsibility: Own the commercial relationship, initiate assessment before onboarding, and act on findings.
Defines the assessment standard, reviews results, and advises on whether risk is acceptable.
Ensures required security terms are in the contract before it is signed.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a current inventory of third parties that hold its information or access its systems.
Each third party has a named internal owner accountable for the relationship.
Security is assessed before a third party is given access to confidential information, proportionate to what they will hold.
Contracts with third parties handling confidential information require them to protect it and to notify {{org}} of a breach.
Third-party access is removed when the engagement ends, and removal is verified rather than assumed.
{{org}} knows which third parties would materially disrupt operations if they became unavailable.
ig2: Third parties are tiered by the sensitivity of what they hold and the impact of their failure, and assessment depth follows that tier.
High-tier third parties are reassessed at least {{review}}, not only at onboarding.
Contracts with high-tier third parties specify a breach notification deadline, a right to audit or to receive assurance evidence, and requirements for subprocessors.
Independent assurance is obtained where available, such as a current SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate, and the scope is checked rather than the logo.
Findings from third-party assessments are tracked to closure or explicitly accepted.
ig3: {{org}} maintains an exit plan for each high-tier third party, covering data return and destruction.
Concentration risk is assessed, so that reliance on a single provider across several critical functions is visible to leadership.
Assurance evidence is validated against {{org}}'s own control requirements rather than accepted at face value.
Third-party incidents are exercised as part of {{org}}'s incident response testing.

policies.exceptions: Engaging a third party without completing assessment requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, and completion of the assessment within a stated period.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident involving a third party.
evidence: The third-party inventory, with tier and named owner
Completed assessments for high-tier third parties
Contract clauses covering security, breach notification, and subprocessors
Evidence that access was removed at the end of an engagement

policies.title: Asset Management Policy
policies.summary: Knowing what {{org}} owns, who is responsible for it, and what happens to it at the end of its life.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} identifies, records, and maintains accountability for the hardware, software, and services it depends on, so that controls can be applied to a known population rather than an assumed one.
policies.scope: All hardware, software, cloud services, and data stores {{org}} owns, leases, or subscribes to, including personally owned devices used for work.

roles.responsibility: Maintains this policy and the standard for what an asset record must contain to be useful for security decisions.
Keeps the asset inventory current through acquisition, change, and disposal, and reconciles it against what is actually connected.
Accept accountability for the assets assigned to them, including their configuration and eventual secure disposal.

ig1: {{org}} maintains an inventory of hardware assets that includes at minimum the asset, its owner, and its location or environment.
{{org}} maintains an inventory of software and cloud services in use, including who authorized each one.
Assets that {{org}} cannot identify or account for are investigated and either recorded or removed from the environment.
Every asset holding confidential information has a named owner accountable for it.
Assets are removed from the inventory only when they have been securely disposed of or returned, and the disposal is recorded.
Storage media are sanitized or destroyed before disposal, resale, or return to a lessor.
Unauthorized software is removed when found, or formally approved and recorded.
ig2: The inventory is reconciled against an automated discovery source at least quarterly, and differences are resolved rather than noted.
Asset records include the classification of the information the asset holds, so protection follows the data.
End-of-life and end-of-support dates are tracked for assets, so replacement is planned rather than forced by an incident.
Cloud services are inventoried with the data they hold and the owner who approved them, including services adopted by individual teams.
Assets connecting to {{org}}'s network are identified, and unrecognized devices are investigated.
ig3: The inventory is maintained close to real time for assets in scope of regulatory obligations.
Asset accuracy is measured, reported, and treated as a control that can fail rather than a housekeeping task.
Disposal of assets holding confidential information is evidenced by certificate or verifiable log.
Software inventory supports answering, within a defined time, which assets run a given component when a vulnerability is announced.

policies.exceptions: An asset may be operated outside this policy only with written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a materially different class of asset or hosting model.
evidence: The current hardware and software inventories
The most recent reconciliation against discovery data
Disposal and sanitization records
Records showing an owner assigned to each asset holding confidential data

policies.title: Authentication and Credential Policy
policies.summary: How people and services prove who they are, and how those credentials are protected.
policies.purpose: This policy sets the requirements for authenticating users and services to {{org}}'s systems, and for the protection of the credentials that make authentication possible.
policies.scope: All authentication to systems {{org}} owns or subscribes to, by workers, contractors, customers, and services, including administrative and emergency access.

roles.responsibility: Sets authentication requirements, approves exceptions, and reviews their continued justification.
Configure their systems to meet these requirements, or document why the system cannot and what compensates.
Protect their own credentials, use the approved multi-factor method, and report suspected compromise immediately.

ig1: Multi-factor authentication is required for all remote access, all administrative access, and all externally reachable services.
Credentials are never shared between individuals, and each person authenticates as themselves.
Default passwords are changed before a system is placed into service.
Passwords meet a documented minimum length, and {{org}} does not require periodic rotation in the absence of evidence of compromise.
Credentials are stored only in an approved password manager, never in documents, spreadsheets, code, or messages.
Accounts are locked or rate limited after a defined number of failed authentication attempts.
Suspected credential compromise triggers immediate reset and review of what that account accessed.
ig2: Multi-factor authentication is required for all access to systems holding confidential information, not only remote access.
Phishing-resistant factors are used for administrative accounts where the platform supports them.
Service and machine credentials are stored in a managed secret store, are rotated on a defined schedule, and are never embedded in source code.
Authentication to {{org}}'s systems is centralized through a single identity provider wherever the system supports it.
Password reset and account recovery processes verify identity in a way that cannot be satisfied with public information.
ig3: Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication is required for all workers, not only administrators.
Credentials appearing in public breach corpora are detected and forced to reset.
Authentication anomalies, such as impossible travel or unusual factor changes, are alerted on and investigated.
Emergency access accounts are held under documented dual control and their use triggers an automatic review.

policies.exceptions: A system that cannot meet these requirements may be used only with written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and a plan with a date to remediate or retire it.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever an authentication method in use is shown to be materially weakened.
evidence: Multi-factor enrollment coverage for workers and administrators
Authentication configuration for systems holding confidential data
Secret store inventory showing rotation dates for service credentials
Records of approved exceptions with their expiry dates

policies.title: Privileged Access Management Policy
policies.summary: Tighter rules for the accounts that can change or destroy things, because those are the accounts attackers want.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how privileged access to {{org}}'s systems is granted, used, monitored, and withdrawn, recognizing that these accounts carry disproportionate risk.
policies.scope: All accounts that can alter system configuration, access confidential data in bulk, change access rights, or bypass logging, on any system {{org}} owns or subscribes to.

roles.responsibility: Defines what counts as privileged in {{org}}'s environment and reviews the population of privileged accounts.
Approve privileged access to their systems and confirm during review that each grant is still required.
Use privileged access only for the task that required it, and never for routine work such as email or browsing.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a current list of every account with privileged access, and who owns it.
Privileged access is granted only where the role requires it, and is approved by the system owner before provisioning.
Privileged accounts are separate from the day-to-day accounts of the same individual.
Multi-factor authentication is required for every privileged account without exception.
Privileged access is revoked the same business day a worker leaves or changes to a role that no longer requires it.
Actions taken with privileged accounts are logged, and the logs cannot be altered by the account that generated them.
ig2: Privileged access is reviewed at least quarterly, more often than standard access, and unjustified grants are removed.
Administrative tasks are performed from a hardened workstation or session dedicated to that purpose.
Vendor and support accounts with privileged access are enabled only for the duration of the work and disabled afterwards.
Shared privileged credentials, where unavoidable, are held in a managed vault that attributes each use to an individual.
Privileged sessions to systems holding confidential data are recorded or monitored.
ig3: Privileged access is granted just in time against an approved request and expires automatically.
No standing privileged access exists for production systems holding confidential information.
Privileged activity is reviewed against expected change records, and unmatched activity is investigated.
Break-glass accounts are sealed, monitored, and tested on a schedule so that their use is always exceptional and always noticed.

policies.exceptions: Standing privileged access beyond what this policy permits requires written approval from {{owner}} and the system owner, a compensating monitoring control, and review at least quarterly.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident involving misuse or compromise of a privileged account.
evidence: The current privileged account inventory
Quarterly privileged access review records
Multi-factor enrollment evidence for privileged accounts
Logs or recordings of privileged sessions for systems holding confidential data

policies.title: Network Security and Segmentation Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} controls what can reach what, so that one compromised host is not the whole estate.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} designs, protects, and segments its networks so that access between systems is deliberate rather than incidental.
policies.scope: All networks {{org}} operates or configures, including cloud virtual networks, remote access, wireless, and any network segment holding confidential information.

roles.responsibility: Approves the segmentation model and reviews whether the rules in force still match it.
Implement and document network controls, and ensure every rule has a recorded business justification.
Declare what network access their systems genuinely require, rather than requesting broad access for convenience.

ig1: Traffic entering and leaving {{org}}'s networks is filtered, and the default posture is to deny what is not explicitly permitted.
Administrative interfaces are not reachable from the public internet without authenticated remote access.
Wireless networks require authentication, and guest wireless is separated from networks carrying {{org}}'s information.
Remote access to internal systems requires an encrypted channel and multi-factor authentication.
Network device configurations are backed up, and changes are recorded.
Every firewall or security group rule has a recorded owner and business justification.
ig2: Systems holding confidential information sit in segments separated from general user networks.
Network rules are reviewed at least {{review}}, and rules that no longer have a justification are removed.
Traffic between segments is restricted to the specific ports and services required, rather than permitted broadly.
Systems that cannot be patched or hardened are isolated so that their exposure does not extend to the wider network.
Outbound traffic is restricted so that a compromised host cannot freely reach arbitrary destinations.
ig3: Access between systems is authenticated and authorized per connection rather than granted by network location.
Segmentation effectiveness is tested at least {{review}}, not assumed from the configuration.
Network traffic within segments is monitored for lateral movement, not only at the perimeter.
Changes to network rules are reconciled against approved change records, and unmatched changes are investigated.

policies.exceptions: A network rule that departs from this policy requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, a compensating control, and an expiry date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} materially changes its hosting model or network architecture.
evidence: The documented segmentation model
Current firewall and security group rules with justifications
The most recent network rule review
Results of any segmentation testing

policies.title: Endpoint and Malware Defense Policy
policies.summary: Protecting the laptops, servers, and mobile devices where most compromises actually begin.
policies.purpose: This policy sets the protections required on devices that access {{org}}'s information, so that a single device compromise is detected and contained rather than becoming an entry point.
policies.scope: All laptops, desktops, servers, mobile devices, and virtual instances that access or hold {{org}}'s information, whether owned by {{org}} or by the individual.

roles.responsibility: Sets the endpoint protection standard and reviews coverage against the asset inventory.
Deploys and maintains endpoint protection, and investigates devices that fall out of compliance.
Keep their devices updated, do not disable required protections, and report loss or suspected compromise immediately.

ig1: Anti-malware protection is deployed on all endpoints that support it, and is configured to update automatically.
Endpoint protection is enabled and cannot be disabled by a standard user.
Devices holding confidential information have full disk encryption enabled.
Devices lock automatically after a period of inactivity and require authentication to unlock.
Lost or stolen devices are reported immediately and can be remotely wiped where the platform supports it.
Endpoint protection coverage is checked against the asset inventory so that unprotected devices are found.
ig2: Endpoint detection and response capability is deployed on endpoints holding or accessing confidential information.
Alerts from endpoint protection are routed to a person or team who is accountable for triaging them within a defined time.
Removable media use is restricted or controlled on devices holding confidential information.
Personally owned devices accessing {{org}}'s information meet a documented minimum standard before access is granted.
Devices that fall out of compliance lose access to confidential systems until they are remediated.
ig3: Application control restricts endpoints to approved software rather than blocking known-bad software only.
Endpoint telemetry is retained centrally for a defined period sufficient to support investigation.
Detection coverage is validated against known techniques rather than assumed from vendor claims.
Time from endpoint alert to triage is measured and reported.

policies.exceptions: A device may operate without a required protection only with written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and an expiry date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a materially different device platform.
evidence: Endpoint protection coverage reconciled against the asset inventory
Encryption status for devices holding confidential data
Alert triage records showing time to response
Records of devices removed from access for non-compliance

policies.title: Secure Configuration Policy
policies.summary: Systems start hardened and stay that way, rather than shipping with whatever the vendor left on.
policies.purpose: This policy requires that systems are configured securely before use and remain so, so that {{org}} is not exposed by defaults chosen for convenience rather than safety.
policies.scope: All operating systems, applications, network devices, cloud services, and container images {{org}} deploys or subscribes to.

roles.responsibility: Approves the configuration baselines and reviews evidence that systems conform to them.
Apply the baseline to their systems and justify any documented deviation.
Maintains the baselines against vendor and benchmark updates and reports drift.

ig1: {{org}} maintains documented secure configuration baselines for the platforms it operates.
Baselines are applied before a system is placed into service, not retrofitted afterwards.
Default accounts, sample content, and unnecessary services are removed or disabled during build.
Administrative interfaces and management ports are not exposed beyond what the system requires.
Configuration changes are recorded so that the current state of a system can be explained.
Baselines are based on a recognized benchmark where one exists for the platform.
ig2: Conformance to baseline is checked automatically at least {{review}}, and drift is remediated or documented as an accepted deviation.
Baselines are reviewed against updated vendor guidance and benchmark releases at least {{review}}.
Cloud service configurations are covered by baselines to the same standard as operating systems.
Container and machine images are built from a controlled source and rebuilt rather than patched in place.
Deviations from baseline are recorded with an owner, a reason, and a review date.
ig3: Configuration state is enforced automatically, so that drift is corrected rather than only reported.
Infrastructure is defined as code and changes flow through review, so that configuration has a reviewable history.
Baseline conformance is measured and reported as a percentage of the estate, not as a binary.
New platform types cannot enter production until a baseline exists for them.

policies.exceptions: A deviation from baseline requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason and compensating control, and a review date no longer than one cycle away.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a platform for which no baseline exists.
evidence: The current configuration baselines and their source benchmarks
Conformance scan results for the review period
The register of approved deviations
Build records showing baseline applied before service

policies.title: Vulnerability and Patch Management Policy
policies.summary: Finding weaknesses on a schedule and fixing them within a deadline that matches their severity.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} identifies, prioritizes, and remediates technical vulnerabilities, so that exposure is closed on a timeline rather than when convenient.
policies.scope: All systems, applications, containers, and network devices {{org}} operates, and the third-party components within them.

roles.responsibility: Sets remediation deadlines by severity, reports on overdue items, and escalates unremediated critical exposure.
Remediate vulnerabilities in their systems within the required timeframe or obtain a documented exception.
Runs scanning, maintains its coverage against the asset inventory, and distributes results to owners.

ig1: Security updates are applied to operating systems and applications on a defined schedule.
Critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems are remediated within a documented deadline.
{{org}} runs authenticated vulnerability scanning at least monthly against its systems.
Scanning coverage is reconciled against the asset inventory so that unscanned systems are visible.
Vulnerabilities are assigned to a named owner for remediation rather than reported to nobody in particular.
Systems that can no longer receive security updates are identified and either replaced or isolated.
ig2: Remediation deadlines are defined per severity and per exposure, and performance against them is reported.
Third-party and open-source components are inventoried, and vulnerabilities in them are tracked to the same deadlines.
Vulnerabilities that cannot be remediated within the deadline require a documented exception with a compensating control.
Scanning includes authenticated checks of cloud service configuration, not only network-reachable services.
Remediation is verified by rescan rather than closed on assertion.
ig3: Prioritization accounts for exploitability and business exposure, not severity score alone.
{{org}} can determine which systems run a given component within a defined time of a vulnerability being announced.
Penetration testing is performed at least {{review}} by a party independent of those who built the system.
Mean time to remediate is measured by severity and reported to leadership as a trend.

policies.exceptions: A vulnerability that cannot be remediated within its deadline requires written approval from {{owner}}, a compensating control, and a documented remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident that exploited a known unremediated vulnerability.
evidence: Scan results and coverage against the asset inventory
Remediation performance against deadlines by severity
The register of approved vulnerability exceptions
The most recent penetration test report and its remediation status

policies.title: Encryption and Key Management Policy
policies.summary: Where encryption is required, which algorithms are acceptable, and how keys are looked after.
policies.purpose: This policy defines where {{org}} requires encryption, which cryptographic methods are approved, and how keys are generated, stored, rotated, and retired.
policies.scope: All {{org}} information in transit and at rest, and all cryptographic keys and certificates used to protect it.

roles.responsibility: Approves the list of acceptable algorithms and key lengths, and reviews it against current guidance.
Implement approved cryptography in their systems and record where keys are held.
Manages the key and certificate lifecycle, including expiry monitoring and rotation.

ig1: Confidential information is encrypted in transit over any network {{org}} does not control.
Confidential information is encrypted at rest on portable devices and removable media.
{{org}} maintains a documented list of approved algorithms and minimum key lengths, and does not use deprecated algorithms.
Certificates and keys are inventoried with their expiry dates, and expiry is monitored so that services do not fail unexpectedly.
Private keys are never transmitted or stored in plaintext, including in source code or configuration files.
Encryption is enabled using platform-native capability rather than custom cryptographic implementations.
ig2: Confidential information is encrypted at rest on servers and in cloud storage wherever the platform supports it.
Keys are stored in a managed key store separated from the data they protect, with access restricted and logged.
Keys have a defined lifetime and are rotated on schedule, and rotation is tested rather than assumed to work.
Internal traffic carrying confidential information is encrypted, not only traffic crossing the perimeter.
Compromise of a key triggers a documented response including re-encryption where required.
ig3: Key management operations require dual control for keys protecting the most sensitive information.
{{org}} maintains an inventory of where cryptography is used sufficient to plan an algorithm migration.
Cryptographic configuration is validated by independent testing rather than by configuration review alone.
Key access is monitored, and use outside expected patterns is investigated.

policies.exceptions: Use of a non-approved algorithm or an unencrypted path for confidential information requires written approval from {{owner}}, a compensating control, and a documented remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever an algorithm in use is deprecated by recognized guidance.
evidence: The approved algorithm and key length standard
The certificate and key inventory with expiry dates
Key rotation records
Encryption configuration for systems holding confidential data

policies.title: Logging, Monitoring, and Detection Policy
policies.summary: Collecting the evidence needed to notice an incident and to reconstruct it afterwards.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes what {{org}} logs, how long it keeps logs, and how those logs are monitored, so that security events can be detected and investigated.
policies.scope: All systems, applications, and services {{org}} operates or subscribes to that process confidential information or control access to it.

roles.responsibility: Defines what must be logged, sets retention, and reviews whether detection coverage matches {{org}}'s risks.
Ensure their systems produce the required logs and forward them to the central store.
Maintains log collection, monitors for gaps in ingestion, and preserves logs against alteration.

ig1: Authentication successes and failures, and administrative actions, are logged on systems holding confidential information.
Logs are retained for a documented minimum period sufficient to investigate an incident discovered late.
System clocks are synchronized to a common time source so that events across systems can be correlated.
Logs are stored so that the account generating an event cannot alter or delete the record of it.
A named individual is responsible for reviewing security-relevant events on a defined cadence.
Loss of logging from a system in scope is itself treated as an event to investigate.
ig2: Logs from systems holding confidential information are forwarded to a central store separate from the systems that produce them.
Detection rules exist for the events {{org}} has decided matter, and each rule has a documented response.
Alerts are routed to a person or team accountable for triaging them within a defined time.
Log coverage is reconciled against the asset inventory so that systems silently not logging are found.
Retention meets the longest applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, not merely operational convenience.
ig3: Detection coverage is mapped against a recognized adversary technique catalogue, and gaps are tracked.
Detection rules are tested by simulating the activity they are meant to catch.
Time from event to alert and from alert to triage is measured and reported.
Log integrity is verifiable, so that evidence would withstand challenge.

policies.exceptions: A system in scope that cannot produce required logs may operate only with written approval from {{owner}}, a compensating detective control, and a documented remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where insufficient logging hindered investigation.
evidence: The logging standard stating what must be logged and for how long
Log coverage reconciled against the asset inventory
Detection rules and their documented responses
Alert triage records showing time to response

policies.title: Email and Web Protection Policy
policies.summary: Hardening the two channels most attacks arrive through.
policies.purpose: This policy sets the protections required on {{org}}'s email and web access, which are the most common initial access paths for attackers.
policies.scope: All email sent or received using {{org}}'s domains, and all web access from {{org}}'s managed devices and networks.

roles.responsibility: Sets the required email and web protections and reviews their effectiveness against reported phishing.
Configures and maintains mail authentication, filtering, and web protections.
Report suspected phishing through the provided mechanism rather than deleting it silently.

ig1: {{org}} publishes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for every domain it sends mail from.
Inbound mail is filtered for malicious content and known malicious senders.
Workers have a simple, always-available way to report a suspected phishing message.
Externally originated mail is visibly marked so recipients can tell it did not come from inside {{org}}.
Web access from managed devices is filtered against known malicious destinations.
Domains {{org}} owns but does not send mail from are configured so they cannot be used to send mail.
ig2: DMARC is set to a policy that instructs receivers to reject or quarantine failures, not merely to report them.
Reported phishing is triaged within a defined time, and confirmed messages are removed from other recipients' mailboxes.
Attachments and links are analyzed before delivery or on click, rather than trusted on sender reputation alone.
Mail forwarding rules to external addresses are restricted or alerted on, since they are a common exfiltration path.
Web filtering categories are reviewed so that the block list reflects {{org}}'s actual risk rather than defaults.
ig3: Phishing simulations are run at least {{review}}, and results drive targeted training rather than blame.
DMARC aggregate reports are monitored, so that abuse of {{org}}'s domains is detected.
Time from phishing report to removal from other mailboxes is measured and reported.
Detection exists for successful phishing, not only for attempted delivery.

policies.exceptions: A relaxation of these protections requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where email or web was the initial access path.
evidence: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for all owned domains
The DMARC enforcement policy in effect
Phishing report triage times for the review period
Phishing simulation results and the training that followed

policies.title: Secure Development Policy
policies.summary: Building security into software {{org}} writes, rather than testing for it at the end.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security requirements for software {{org}} develops or substantially customizes, so that defects are prevented and found early rather than discovered in production.
policies.scope: All software {{org}} writes, commissions, or materially customizes, including internal tools, infrastructure code, and scripts that handle confidential information.

roles.responsibility: Sets secure development requirements, reviews findings from testing, and advises on risk acceptance for unremediated defects.
Ensure their teams follow these requirements and that security findings are prioritized alongside functional work.
Write code to the standard, address findings in their own work, and never commit credentials to source control.

ig1: Source code is held in version control, and production changes are traceable to a commit and an author.
Credentials, keys, and tokens are never committed to source control, and repositories are scanned to enforce this.
Code changes are reviewed by someone other than the author before reaching production.
Third-party components are inventoried, and components with known vulnerabilities are updated.
Development and test environments do not use unmasked production data holding confidential information.
Developers receive secure development training relevant to the languages and platforms they use.
ig2: Automated security testing runs in the build pipeline, covering both first-party code and dependencies.
Findings above a defined severity block release, rather than being logged for later.
Applications handling confidential information are threat modeled before significant architectural change.
A software bill of materials is produced for applications {{org}} ships or operates in production.
Security requirements are defined at the start of a project rather than assessed at the end.
ig3: Applications handling confidential information are tested by an independent party at least {{review}}.
Build pipelines and artifact repositories are protected as production systems, since they can inject code into production.
Build provenance is recorded so that a deployed artifact can be traced to the source and process that produced it.
Defect escape rate and time to remediate are measured and reported.

policies.exceptions: Releasing with an unremediated finding above the blocking threshold requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and a remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a materially different development platform or delivery model.
evidence: Branch protection and code review settings
Security testing results from the build pipeline
Dependency inventory and its vulnerability status
Independent application test reports and remediation status

policies.title: Backup and Recovery Policy
policies.summary: Copies that survive the event that destroyed the original, and that are proven to restore.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} backs up its information and validates that it can be restored, so that recovery is a tested capability rather than an assumption.
policies.scope: All systems and information required to operate {{org}}, including data held in cloud services where the provider does not guarantee recovery to {{org}}'s requirements.

roles.responsibility: Sets backup and retention requirements based on recovery objectives and reviews restore test results.
Define the recovery point and recovery time objectives their system requires and confirm backups meet them.
Runs backups, monitors for failures, and performs restore testing on schedule.

ig1: Systems and information required to operate {{org}} are backed up on a defined schedule.
At least one backup copy is held offline, off-site, or in an account separate from the systems it protects.
Backups of confidential information are encrypted.
Backup failures generate an alert to a named owner rather than failing silently.
A restore is tested at least {{review}}, and the test is recorded with its outcome.
Access to backups and to backup configuration is restricted to a small, documented set of accounts.
ig2: Recovery point and recovery time objectives are documented per system and backup schedules are set to meet them.
Backup copies are protected against deletion or encryption by an attacker who has compromised production credentials.
Restore testing covers full system recovery, not only individual file restoration.
Data held in cloud services is backed up where the provider's native retention does not meet {{org}}'s objectives.
Backup retention meets the longest applicable regulatory or contractual obligation.
ig3: Restore testing is performed against the documented recovery time objective, and shortfalls are treated as findings.
At least one backup copy is immutable for a defined period.
Recovery is exercised as part of incident response testing, using the backups that would actually be used.
Backup integrity is verified rather than inferred from job success.

policies.exceptions: A system operating without backups meeting this policy requires written approval from {{owner}}, an accepted recovery risk recorded in the risk register, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever recovery objectives change or a restore test fails to meet them.
evidence: Backup schedules and their coverage against critical systems
Restore test records with dates and outcomes
Evidence that a copy is isolated from production credentials
Documented recovery objectives per system

policies.title: Business Continuity Policy
policies.summary: Keeping {{org}} running through disruption, and knowing in advance what has to come back first.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} prepares to continue operating through significant disruption, and how it decides what to restore first.
policies.scope: All business processes {{org}} depends on and the systems, people, facilities, and suppliers that support them.

roles.responsibility: Approves recovery priorities and the level of disruption {{org}} is prepared to accept.
Maintains this policy and coordinates continuity planning and exercises across the business.
Identify what their process requires to operate and document how it would run in degraded conditions.

ig1: {{org}} has identified the business processes it cannot operate without and the systems each one depends on.
Recovery priorities are documented and approved by leadership before an event, not decided during one.
Continuity and recovery plans record who does what, and are reachable when normal systems are unavailable.
Contact details for staff, key suppliers, and customers are maintained and accessible outside primary systems.
Plans state how the business would operate manually or in degraded mode where that is possible.
Plans are reviewed at least {{review}} and after any material change to the business.
ig2: A business impact analysis is performed at least {{review}}, quantifying the impact of losing each critical process over time.
Recovery time and recovery point objectives are set per process from that analysis, and systems are provisioned to meet them.
Continuity plans are exercised at least {{review}}, and findings are tracked to closure.
Dependencies on single suppliers or single locations for critical processes are documented and escalated to leadership.
Plans cover loss of key personnel, not only loss of systems or facilities.
ig3: Exercises include scenarios where the primary recovery option is unavailable.
Achieved recovery times from exercises are compared to objectives, and shortfalls are treated as findings.
Continuity arrangements with critical suppliers are validated rather than accepted on assertion.
Continuity requirements are considered before adopting a new critical system or supplier.

policies.exceptions: Operating a critical process without a documented continuity plan requires written approval from leadership, an accepted risk recorded in the risk register, and a date by which a plan will exist.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, after any significant disruption, and after any exercise that identifies a material gap.
evidence: The list of critical processes and their dependencies
The most recent business impact analysis
Exercise records and the findings they produced
Documented recovery objectives approved by leadership

policies.title: Security Awareness and Training Policy
policies.summary: Making sure people know what is expected of them, in terms relevant to their actual job.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security training {{org}} provides, so that workers understand the risks relevant to their role and what they are expected to do about them.
policies.scope: All workers and contractors with access to {{org}}'s information or systems, including those in roles with elevated privileges or specialized responsibilities.

roles.responsibility: Defines the training programme, keeps content current with the threats {{org}} actually faces, and reports completion.
Enrolls new joiners before or on their start date and tracks completion as a condition of continued access.
Ensure their teams complete required training and reinforce expectations in day-to-day work.

ig1: Every worker completes security awareness training on joining and at least {{review}} thereafter.
Training covers how to recognize and report phishing, how to handle confidential information, and how to report an incident.
Completion is tracked, and non-completion is escalated rather than ignored.
Workers are told which behaviours are prohibited and what the consequences of violation are.
Training content is reviewed at least {{review}} so that it reflects current threats rather than last decade's.
New joiners acknowledge {{org}}'s security policies as part of onboarding.
ig2: Roles with elevated risk receive additional training specific to their responsibilities, such as developers and administrators.
Phishing simulation results inform who receives targeted follow-up training.
Training includes {{org}}'s own incident reporting route and named contacts, not generic advice.
Workers handling regulated information receive training on the specific obligations that attach to it.
Awareness activity happens between annual training, rather than only once a year.
ig3: Training effectiveness is measured through behaviour, such as reporting rates and simulation outcomes, not completion alone.
Leadership and those with authority to approve payments or access receive training on the attacks that target them specifically.
Security expectations are included in role descriptions and performance conversations for roles with security responsibilities.
The programme is adjusted based on the incidents and near misses {{org}} actually experiences.

policies.exceptions: A worker may retain access without current training only with written approval from {{owner}}, for a stated period, and with a completion date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where a lack of awareness was a contributing factor.
evidence: Training completion records for the review period
The current training content and its last review date
Phishing simulation results and follow-up training records
Onboarding records showing policy acknowledgement

policies.title: Physical and Environmental Security Policy
policies.summary: Controlling who can physically reach systems and information, and protecting them from their environment.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} restricts physical access to its facilities, systems, and information, and protects them from environmental hazards.
policies.scope: All facilities {{org}} occupies, any equipment holding {{org}}'s information wherever it is located, and the working environments of remote workers to the extent {{org}} can set requirements.

roles.responsibility: Sets physical security requirements for areas holding confidential information and reviews access records.
Administers physical access, maintains visitor records, and reports anomalies.
Do not admit unbadged individuals, secure their workspace, and protect equipment when working outside {{org}}'s facilities.

ig1: Physical access to areas holding systems or confidential information is restricted to authorized individuals.
Visitors to areas holding confidential information are recorded and accompanied.
Physical access is revoked on the same schedule as system access when a worker leaves.
Confidential information on paper is secured when unattended and disposed of by shredding or a secure disposal service.
Devices are not left unattended in public places, and screens are locked when the user steps away.
Equipment holding confidential information is protected from obvious environmental risks such as water and heat.
ig2: Physical access rights are reviewed at least {{review}}, and access that is no longer required is removed.
Physical access to areas holding confidential information is logged, and logs are retained for a defined period.
Deliveries and loading areas are separated from areas holding systems and confidential information.
Requirements for remote and home working are documented, covering how equipment and information are protected outside {{org}}'s facilities.
Server and network equipment areas have environmental protection appropriate to the value of what they hold.
ig3: Physical access logs are reviewed against expected activity, and anomalies are investigated.
Physical access controls to critical areas are tested rather than assumed effective.
Environmental monitoring alerts on conditions that threaten equipment before failure occurs.
Facilities holding the most sensitive information require more than one factor for physical entry.

policies.exceptions: Physical access arrangements departing from this policy require written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} changes premises or materially changes its remote working model.
evidence: Physical access authorization lists for restricted areas
Visitor records for the review period
The most recent physical access review
Secure disposal records for paper holding confidential information

policies.title: Threat Intelligence and Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
policies.summary: Staying informed about what is being exploited, and giving outsiders a way to tell {{org}} about a flaw.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} keeps informed about threats relevant to it, and how it receives and handles vulnerability reports from outside the organization.
policies.scope: Threat information relevant to {{org}}'s technologies, sector, and geography, and all security reports received from external parties including researchers and customers.

roles.responsibility: Monitors relevant threat sources, decides what warrants action, and owns the disclosure process.
Act on advisories affecting technologies {{org}} operates within the timeframe the risk warrants.
Advise on external response where a report becomes public or involves customer information.

ig1: {{org}} subscribes to vendor and authoritative advisories for the technologies it operates.
A named individual reviews advisories on a defined cadence and decides whether action is required.
{{org}} publishes a way for outsiders to report a suspected vulnerability, and that route is monitored.
Reports received from outside are acknowledged within a stated timeframe.
Advisories that require action are tracked to completion rather than read and forgotten.
{{org}} monitors for public reporting of compromise affecting its suppliers.
ig2: Threat information is filtered to what is relevant to {{org}}'s actual technologies and sector, rather than consumed indiscriminately.
A published disclosure policy states what {{org}} commits to, including response timeframes and its position on good-faith research.
Externally reported vulnerabilities enter the same remediation process and deadlines as internally found ones.
Threat information informs detection rules and control priorities rather than being read in isolation.
{{org}} monitors for exposure of its own credentials and data in public breach corpora.
ig3: Threat intelligence is mapped to {{org}}'s detection coverage, so that relevant gaps become work.
{{org}} participates in a sector or peer information sharing arrangement.
Response to externally reported vulnerabilities is measured against published commitments.
Intelligence about attacks on similar organizations drives exercise scenarios.

policies.exceptions: Deviation from published disclosure commitments requires written approval from {{owner}} and, where the report involves customer information, from legal counsel.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any externally reported vulnerability that was not handled within the published timeframe.
evidence: The published vulnerability disclosure route and policy
Records of advisories reviewed and actions taken
External vulnerability reports with acknowledgement and resolution times
Evidence that threat information influenced detection or control priorities

policies.title: Change Management Policy
policies.summary: Changes are reviewed, recorded, and reversible, so that outages and weaknesses are not self-inflicted.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how changes to {{org}}'s systems are proposed, reviewed, approved, and recorded, so that change does not silently introduce risk or unavailability.
policies.scope: All changes to production systems, network and security configuration, access rights, and the pipelines that deploy them.

roles.responsibility: Ensures security implications are considered in change review and that emergency changes are reviewed afterwards.
Assess proposed changes for risk and impact, and approve or reject them before implementation.
Implement only approved changes, record what was done, and execute the rollback if the change fails.

ig1: Changes to production systems are recorded, including what changed, when, by whom, and why.
Changes are approved by someone other than the person implementing them before they reach production.
Changes carry a rollback plan, or a documented reason why rollback is not possible.
Emergency changes may bypass advance approval but are recorded and reviewed afterwards.
Changes to security controls, including firewall rules and access rights, follow this process.
Failed changes are recorded with their impact so that repeated failure modes become visible.
ig2: Change records are retained and can be reconciled against what actually changed in the environment.
Security review is required for changes affecting systems holding confidential information or controls that protect them.
Changes are tested in a non-production environment before production where the change type allows it.
Standard, low-risk changes are pre-approved through a documented definition rather than reviewed individually.
Emergency change volume is monitored, since a high rate usually indicates a process problem rather than genuine emergencies.
ig3: Detected configuration changes are reconciled against approved change records, and unmatched changes are investigated.
Change success and failure rates are measured and reported.
Automated controls prevent unapproved changes to critical production configuration.
Post-implementation review is required for changes above a defined risk threshold.

policies.exceptions: A change implemented outside this process requires retrospective approval from {{owner}} within a defined period, with the reason recorded.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident caused by an unmanaged or unreviewed change.
evidence: Change records for the review period, with approvals
Emergency change records and their retrospective reviews
Evidence of reconciliation between detected and approved changes
The definition of pre-approved standard changes

policies.title: Personnel Security Policy
policies.summary: Security obligations across the employment lifecycle, from screening to the day someone leaves.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security requirements that apply to workers before, during, and after their engagement with {{org}}.
policies.scope: All employees, contractors, and temporary workers, and any third-party personnel granted access to {{org}}'s information or systems.

roles.responsibility: Runs screening, ensures agreements are signed, and notifies system owners of joiners, movers, and leavers in time to act.
Defines screening requirements proportionate to role risk and confirms access removal on departure.
Confirm what access their reports require, and initiate the leaver process promptly including for involuntary departures.

ig1: Workers accept written confidentiality obligations before being granted access to confidential information.
Workers acknowledge {{org}}'s security policies on joining.
A documented leaver process removes system access, recovers equipment, and revokes physical access.
Managers notify people operations and IT of departures with enough notice for access to be removed on the final day.
Involuntary departures trigger immediate access removal, coordinated with the departure itself.
Confidentiality obligations continue after the engagement ends, and workers are reminded of this on departure.
ig2: Background screening proportionate to role risk is completed before access to confidential information is granted.
Role changes trigger an access review, so that permissions accumulated in a previous role are removed.
Contractors and third-party personnel are subject to equivalent requirements, evidenced through their employer where {{org}} does not screen directly.
Security responsibilities are stated in role descriptions for roles that carry them.
Departure checklists are completed and retained, rather than assumed done.
ig3: Screening for roles with the highest access is repeated on a defined cycle rather than only at hire.
Access removal on departure is verified against the account inventory rather than assumed from the checklist.
Departures of workers with privileged access trigger a review of their recent activity.
Time from departure to complete access removal is measured and reported.

policies.exceptions: Granting access before screening or agreements are complete requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, and a completion date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} materially changes how it engages workers.
evidence: Signed confidentiality agreements and policy acknowledgements
Screening records appropriate to role risk
Completed leaver checklists with access removal timing
Evidence of access review following role changes

policies.title: Compliance and Audit Policy
policies.summary: Knowing which obligations apply, and checking that {{org}} actually meets them.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} identifies the legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations that apply to it, and how it verifies that its controls satisfy them.
policies.scope: All legal, regulatory, contractual, and certification obligations relating to information security and privacy that apply to {{org}}.

roles.responsibility: Accepts accountability for compliance and provides the resource needed to meet identified obligations.
Maintains the register of obligations, coordinates assessment against them, and reports findings and status.
Identify obligations arising from law and from customer contracts and communicate them to {{owner}}.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a register of the security and privacy obligations that apply to it, with a named owner for each.
The register records which framework or regulation each obligation comes from, so that requirements can be traced to a source.
Obligations arising from customer contracts are captured, not only those arising from law.
{{org}} performs a documented self-assessment against its primary framework at least {{review}}.
Findings from assessments are assigned an owner and a remediation date.
The register is reviewed at least {{review}} so that new obligations are caught.
ig2: Assessment covers control effectiveness and not only control existence.
Findings are tracked to closure, and closure is evidenced rather than asserted.
Overdue findings are escalated to leadership on a defined cadence.
{{org}} retains the evidence an assessor would request, organized so it can be produced without a fire drill.
Changes in regulation affecting {{org}} are monitored, and their impact assessed within a defined period.
ig3: An independent party assesses {{org}}'s controls at least {{review}}, and reports without filtering through the assessed function.
Control effectiveness is measured continuously where possible, rather than only at assessment time.
Compliance status is reported to leadership with trends, not only point-in-time results.
Evidence collection is automated where the control produces machine-readable output.

policies.exceptions: Accepting a known gap against an identified obligation requires written approval from executive leadership, recording in the risk register, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} becomes subject to a new regulation, certification, or material customer obligation.
evidence: The register of applicable obligations with owners
The most recent self-assessment against the primary framework
The findings register with owners, dates, and closure evidence
Independent assessment reports where applicable
